what: Landstar arranges freight transport without owning trucks. Independent agents find customers who need goods moved, and independent owner-operators who own their own trucks carry the load. Landstar runs the network, handles the money and takes a cut.
customers: Shippers of all sizes needing truckload freight moved, reached through a network of independent commission agents rather than a company sales force.
money: Freight carried by independent owner-operators and third-party carriers.
Insurance services to its owner-operators and other revenue.
moat: The model is the moat: Landstar owns almost no trucks and employs almost no drivers, so its costs fall automatically when freight volumes fall. Agents and owner-operators are paid a share of each load, which means they bear the downturn alongside the company. That makes it the most resilient business model in trucking.
risks: Revenue has declined sharply, from $7.4B in 2022 to $4.7B in 2025, as freight rates collapsed from pandemic highs.
Reported net income of $160.4M gives a price/earnings ratio of 32.2, which reflects depressed earnings at the bottom of the freight cycle.
Last year’s net margin was 2.4%, the structural reality of freight brokerage where most of the revenue is paid to carriers.
Digital freight platforms are attacking the brokerage layer with technology and capital.
Sixteen analysts average a $178.31 target, about 18% above the current price.
opportunities: Essentially no debt — $615,000 against $452.2M of cash — which is extraordinary for a transport company.
The variable cost model means Landstar remains profitable through freight downturns that destroy asset-based carriers.
Agents and owner-operators are paid per load, so costs fall automatically with volumes rather than needing restructuring.
Free cash flow of $157.6M even at the bottom of the cycle shows the model’s resilience.
Operating leverage is substantial when freight rates recover, because the cost base does not rise proportionally.
watch: Loads hauled and revenue per load. Revenue combines volume and rate, and the two move for different reasons — volume tells you about the economy, rate about capacity.
view: Landstar has the best business model in trucking and it is worth being precise about why. It owns almost no trucks and employs almost no drivers. Independent agents find the freight, independent owner-operators haul it, and both are paid a share of each load. So when freight volumes collapse — as they have, with revenue falling from $7.4 billion to $4.7 billion — Landstar’s costs fall automatically. There is no fleet sitting idle, no drivers to lay off, no restructuring charge. The business shrinks and stays profitable.

Compare that with an asset-based carrier, which owns the trucks, employs the drivers, and watches its fixed costs eat the earnings when loads disappear. The freight recession of the last few years has been brutal for asset carriers and merely unpleasant for Landstar. A balance sheet with $615,000 of debt against $452 million of cash is the visible result of a model that never needs to borrow against a fleet.

The reported figures are trough figures and should be read as such. A price/earnings ratio of 32.2 on $160 million of net income reflects earnings at the bottom of a cycle, not an expensive stock — and the same operating leverage works in reverse when rates recover, because the cost base does not rise proportionally with the freight.

The genuine competitive question is whether technology erodes the brokerage layer. Digital freight platforms have raised enormous capital to match loads to trucks algorithmically, and in principle that is exactly what Landstar’s agents do by relationship. In practice the agent network has proven more durable than the disruptors expected, because freight matching involves judgement, trust and problem-solving that software has handled poorly. But the pressure is real and the capital behind it is patient. Loads hauled and revenue per load are the two numbers; the first is the economy and the second is capacity.
bull: Freight rates recover against a variable cost base, operating leverage lifts trough earnings sharply, and a debt-free model compounds through every cycle.
bear: The freight recession drags on while digital platforms erode the agent-based brokerage layer with cheaper algorithmic matching.
